facts.text: Most young people get their National Insurance number by letter shortly before they turn 16.
Most people can earn some money each tax year before paying Income Tax (the Personal Allowance). Check gov.uk for this year's amount.
Your tax code tells your employer how much tax-free pay you get. If it looks wrong, contact HMRC.
You usually can't take out credit until you're 18, so most credit files start around then.
Lenders use the electoral register to confirm who you are and where you live. The age you can register and vote differs across the UK nations, so check gov.uk/register-to-vote.
Missed payments usually stay on a credit file for six years.
In the UK the total interest and fees on a payday loan are capped at the amount you borrowed, but they're still a very expensive way to borrow.
Buy now pay later is borrowing. Missing payments can mean late fees and, with some providers, a mark on your credit file.
If you think a call or message about your bank is a scam, hang up and call 159 to reach your bank safely. Not every bank uses 159, so you can also use the number on the back of your card.
Report fraud to your bank straight away, then to the police's fraud reporting service for your part of the UK.
Letting someone move money through your account is money muling. It's a crime, even if you're told it's a 'job', and it can get your bank account closed.
A phone contract with a handset is usually a credit agreement, so missed payments can show on your credit file.
In England and Wales, landlords must protect a tenancy deposit in a government-approved scheme. Rules differ in Scotland and Northern Ireland.
Some people get a council tax discount or don't pay it at all, for example if everyone in the home is a full-time student.
Many broadband and mobile companies offer cheaper 'social tariffs' to people on certain benefits.
Free, confidential debt advice is available from charities such as Citizens Advice, StepChange and National Debtline, and from MoneyHelper.
Free online benefits calculators can show what support you might be able to get.
Savings in UK banks are protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) up to a limit per person, per bank.

chapters.title: Needs, wants and your first budget
chapters.summary: Tell needs from wants and make a plan for payday.

levels.title: Payday plan
levels.persona: Aisha, 17, works in a café. Her hours change every week.

steps.prompt: Payday! Your shifts were short this month, so you've been paid less than usual. What do you do first?

options.text: List my needs first: bus fares, my phone share and food at college
options.explanation: Covering needs first means a short month doesn't turn into missed bills.

options.text: Spend as normal and hope next month is better
options.explanation: When income goes up and down, planning for the low months protects you.

options.text: Put a little aside first, even £5
options.explanation: Saving a small amount first builds the habit, whatever you earn.

steps.prompt: Which of these is a need?

options.text: A bus pass to get to college
options.explanation: Getting to college or work is a need. The others are wants: nice, but you can live without them.

options.text: New trainers when yours are fine
options.explanation: Trainers that still work are a want right now. A need is something you can't do without.
Streaming is a want. It's fine to have wants, just after needs.
A takeaway is a want. Food is a need, but takeaways cost more.

steps.prompt: A friend's birthday meal costs £25, but you planned £15 for fun this month.

options.text: Suggest a cheaper plan, or just go for dessert
options.explanation: Being honest about your budget is a skill, and friends usually get it.
That's OK sometimes, but it means cutting something else this month.

options.text: Skip it and send a card
options.explanation: Also fine. The point is deciding with your budget, not on the spot.

steps.prompt: A budget is only useful if you have lots of money.

options.explanation: False. A budget matters most when money is tight. It's just a plan for the money you have.
False. A budget matters most when money is tight. It's just a plan for the money you have.

learned: Cover needs before wants.
Plan for your lowest-paid months, not your best.
Saving a little first works on any income.

levels.title: Sharing a flat

steps.prompt: Your sister asks you to put £20 a week towards food shopping. How do you plan for it?

options.text: Add it to my budget as a fixed weekly cost
options.explanation: Treating it like a bill means it never catches you out.
Paying late puts pressure on the people you live with, and it's a habit lenders notice later.

options.text: Ask to pay less this month and say why
options.explanation: Talking early is much better than missing a payment.

steps.prompt: Bus fares go up by 50p a trip.

options.text: Work out the new monthly cost and adjust my budget
options.explanation: Small price rises add up over a month, so updating your plan keeps it real.
50p a trip, twice a day, five days a week is about £20 a month.

options.text: Check for a cheaper weekly or student ticket
options.explanation: Capped and student tickets can save a lot. It's always worth checking.

steps.prompt: What's the simplest way to start a budget?

options.text: Write down the money coming in and going out
options.explanation: That's it. Everything else builds on knowing your money in and out.
Tools help, but the first step is just knowing what comes in and goes out.
Starting now, with whatever you have, is what builds the habit.

learned: Treat shared costs like bills.
Small price rises add up: update your plan.
A budget is money in vs money out.

steps.prompt: Your phone screen cracks. A repair shop quotes £60.

options.text: Check if any insurance or warranty covers it first
options.explanation: Always check what cover you already have before paying.

options.text: Ask for quotes and choose a cheaper, trusted repair
options.explanation: Comparing prices is a simple way to save.

options.text: Keep using it cracked for now
options.explanation: That can be sensible if it still works safely, while you save up.

steps.prompt: What's an emergency fund?

options.text: Money set aside for surprises, like repairs
options.explanation: Yes. Even a small fund means a surprise doesn't become a crisis.
That's a savings goal. An emergency fund is only for surprises.

options.text: A loan you take when things go wrong
options.explanation: A loan is borrowing. An emergency fund is your own money.

steps.prompt: You need a big income to build an emergency fund.

options.explanation: False. Putting aside even £1 or £2 a week adds up, and it's the habit that counts.
False. Putting aside even £1 or £2 a week adds up, and it's the habit that counts.

learned: Check existing cover before paying for repairs.
An emergency fund is for surprises only.
Any amount, saved regularly, builds a buffer.

options.text: The yearly cost of borrowing, including interest and most fees
options.explanation: APR lets you compare the cost of different credit. Higher APR means more expensive.

options.text: How much you'll earn on savings
options.explanation: That's AER. APR is the cost of borrowing.

True. An overdraft lets you spend money you don't have, and you'll usually pay interest on it.

options.text: Work out the total cost and whether I can repay it
